slides.title: A connection gives bytes, not a completed agreement
keyPoints: A socket is an owned endpoint
The protocol gives received bytes meaning
Transport progress is not transaction completion
slides.narration: Imagine a client sending two orders over one connection. The operating system can deliver the beginning of the first order, then its end together with the next order. Nothing is wrong with the connection. The missing boundary is the application message format, called framing. This chapter separates endpoint setup from interpretation: creating or connecting a socket does not validate a request, authorize an action, or prove the peer completed it. Start with a written format, a size limit, and completion rules. Those rules let us decide whether a short read means wait, reject, or finish without guessing from buffer size.

slides.title: A tiny line protocol preserves the unfinished tail
keyPoints: Append new bytes to connection state
Extract only complete newline-terminated messages
Keep bytes after the last complete message
slides.narration: This is a deterministic parser model, not a socket measurement. Three supplied chunks divide the word HELLO and then divide BYE across different arrival boundaries. The parser appends each chunk, searches for a newline, prints only the complete line, and removes exactly those consumed bytes. The output is HELLO followed by BYE, with a final tail count of zero. The loop inside the loop matters because one chunk can complete more than one message. If the final newline were absent, the tail would remain buffered instead of being invented as a complete request. A production protocol also needs a bound on this buffer.

slides.title: The delimiter can also be ordinary payload
keyPoints: A newline protocol needs escaping or a restricted alphabet
A length prefix permits newline bytes in the payload
Decode lengths before using them
slides.narration: The simple line protocol works only if newline has one agreed meaning. Our payload is A, newline, B. Adding a terminating newline now makes a receiver see two lines even though the sender intended one payload. The second representation uses two explicit header bytes containing the length three, followed by the same three payload bytes. Decoding the header produces three regardless of the machine's native integer layout. The output therefore reports two delimiter messages but three length-framed payload bytes. This program models serialization; it does not receive data. Real input must be checked for a complete header, an allowed length, and a complete body before slicing it.

slides.title: The listener and accepted connection have different jobs
keyPoints: socket creates an endpoint; bind chooses its local address
listen enables accepting connections
accept returns a separate connected descriptor
slides.narration: Picture a workshop with one reception desk and several conversations. The listening socket is the reception desk. accept returns another descriptor for one conversation, while the listener stays available for the next client. Reading application bytes from the listener confuses those roles. Each returned descriptor needs an owner that closes it on both success and rejection. For a local lab, binding loopback limits who can reach the service; port zero asks the operating system to select an available port. Neither choice proves requests are valid. The source example deliberately separates the setup sequence from the later framing and transfer helpers.

slides.title: Client/server architecture
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A server offers a service through a known or discovered endpoint; a client initiates a request.
Once connected, both sides can send and receive according to the application protocol.
Roles do not change the need to validate all incoming data.
Define request and response formats before writing the main loop.
slides.narration:
A server offers a service through a known or discovered endpoint; a client initiates a request. Once connected, both sides can send and receive according to the application protocol. Roles do not change the need to validate all incoming data. Define request and response formats before writing the main loop. Specify maximum lengths, supported versions, how errors are represented, and whether a connection carries one message or many. slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The reusable header below owns descriptors, bounds frames to 1024 bytes, handles partial transfers and EINTR , and treats premature EOF as failure.
It uses Linux’s MSG_NOSIGNAL for sends so that a broken connection becomes an error instead of terminating the process through SIGPIPE .
The small socket timeouts are per-operation limits, not a complete whole-request deadline policy.

slides.title: Short progress and interrupted calls need explicit state
keyPoints: A positive count advances an offset
EINTR may require a retry under the operation’s contract
EOF halfway through a frame is truncation
slides.narration: Suppose a four-byte header arrives as one byte, then two, then one. The receiver must remember an offset of one, then three, then four before decoding the header. A positive return counts progress, not necessarily completion. A zero stream read indicates EOF: between messages it may be normal closure, but halfway through a header or body it is a truncated frame. A negative result requires the documented error handling, including interruption and would-block cases where applicable. Writing the offset loop once in a checked helper keeps every caller from inventing a slightly different partial-transfer policy.

slides.title: A length is both a parsing field and a resource request
keyPoints: Validate the protocol maximum before allocation
Distinguish incomplete from invalid
Retain the next message’s unconsumed bytes
slides.narration: An advertised length is not permission to allocate that many bytes. If a service allows at most one kilobyte, a million-byte prefix should be rejected before allocating the body buffer. An allowed length with too few bytes available is a different condition: incomplete input can become valid after another read. The small workshop parser makes that distinction with an optional complete frame and a separate invalid-length error. It also returns a consumed count so the connection can retain later messages. Clearing the entire buffer after one parse would silently discard a valid second frame or its beginning.

question.prompt: Why should an oversized prefix be rejected even when its body has not arrived?
question.answer: The prefix already violates the resource contract. Waiting or allocating first adds avoidable memory and connection pressure.

slides.title: Deadlines bound a request, not merely one system call
keyPoints: Per-operation timeouts restart across operations
A slow peer can stretch a sequence of successful reads
Track an overall completion budget
slides.narration: Consider a request that needs ten reads. A one-second timeout on each read does not automatically make the whole request finish within one second. A peer that makes tiny progress just before each timeout can keep the request open much longer. The source's small socket timeouts bound individual operations for the lab; they are not a complete request-deadline policy. A service usually needs an overall deadline or progress rule as well as a size limit. That policy belongs to connection state, alongside partial headers, pending output, and whether the peer has ended its sending direction.

slides.title: Connection setup has its own incomplete state
keyPoints: Nonblocking connect may report in-progress
Readiness must be followed by the documented socket-error check
Retry needs a limit and a delay policy
slides.narration: A nonblocking connect can begin an attempt without completing it. Treating the in-progress result as success lets application writes run before the connection is known to be usable. The program must wait for the relevant readiness and inspect the socket error state according to the interface. Connection failures are expected events, not rare impossibilities: the peer may be absent or unavailable. Retrying forever can consume descriptors, memory, and downstream capacity. A maintainable client makes attempt count, delay, deadline, and retryable operations explicit so a remote outage does not become uncontrolled local work.

The declared length must satisfy both the application maximum and the available byte extent. A short stream read is not a complete message.
Construct owned message text from exactly the declared payload range. The lab additionally returns the consumed count so a following frame is not accidentally discarded.
theory.what: TCP does not preserve application messages. The first received byte states the payload length. This fixture already contains a header; a general parser must check for it before this access.
theory.where: A byte-stream model delivers a length-prefixed message as two fragments. Assemble a complete frame before interpreting it.
theory.why: The frame is incomplete even though a read delivered data. Buffering must retain earlier bytes until the frame is complete. The model caps lengths at 8. A real parser also retains any following frame bytes and handles EOF or errors mid-frame.
theory.invariant: No payload is interpreted until its complete declared extent is available and within the application limit. Receive-call boundaries are not message boundaries.
theory.risk: Assuming one send matches one recv call confuses stream transport with application framing. In the extended lab: Clear the whole receive buffer after parsing the first frame. Any complete or partial second frame disappears.

slides.title: Choose a framing contract before choosing a bigger buffer
keyPoints: Delimited text needs escaping and a maximum line length
Fixed records need an agreed fixed size
Length prefixes need byte order and a size maximum
slides.narration: There are several reasonable protocols. A newline format is easy to inspect when the payload alphabet excludes newline or defines escaping. Fixed-size records simplify accumulation when every record truly has the same size. A length prefix supports arbitrary payload bytes but adds header decoding and an untrusted resource request. None becomes correct merely by choosing a large receive buffer. A message can still be split, and several messages can still arrive together. Write tests that vary chunk boundaries independently of message boundaries. That verifies the parser contract rather than one convenient transport schedule.

slides.title: Diagnose transport, framing, and application failures separately
keyPoints: Transport: what byte progress happened?
Framing: is one complete bounded message available?
Application: is that message meaningful and authorized?
slides.narration: When a network operation fails, record the boundary that failed before changing unrelated code. A broken connection is not the same as an oversized frame. A complete bounded frame is not the same as a valid order. A valid order is not proof that its acknowledgment reached the client. Separate statuses make retries and logs meaningful. In this chapter's local fixtures, verify empty and maximum-size frames, oversized prefixes, mid-header EOF, and mid-body EOF. These checks support the byte-stream contract. They do not establish authentication, encryption, internet deployment safety, or a full transaction protocol, which would need their own requirements and tests.
